title: From Golf Greens to the White House: Inside Trump's Unusual Grass Fixation
summary: Picture this: the President of the United States, staring out the Oval Office window, not at global threats but at the lawn. 'You see the grass outside, right?' Donald Trump asked an interviewer just five weeks into his second term. Then he detailed plans to pave over much of it. That moment captures a bizarre pattern: Trump has talked about grass at least 45 times in 18 months—once every 12 days. He's mentioned it more often than the war in Iran, the economy, or the midterm elections. Why the obsession? Trump traces it to his decades as a real estate developer and golf course owner. 'I know a lot about grass because I own a lot of golf courses,' he said. 'If you don't have good grass, you're not in business very long.' Matt Koch, a lawns research fellow for Scotts Miracle-Gro, met with Trump and came away convinced the president is an honorary 'grass nerd.' But there's a twist: while Trump boasts about his grass expertise, he's also tearing it up. He paved a stone patio over part of the Rose Garden, blaming women in high heels who complained their shoes got stuck in the mud. 'The women would be lifting up their shoes, saying, You've destroyed my shoes,' he recounted. For his 80th birthday, a UFC octagon on the South Lawn left it a dusty mess. Now, a sprawling helicopter landing pad is replacing even more turf—Trump says the powerful new Marine One helicopters rip out grass on landing. 'Half of the grass was sitting in front of the Oval Office front door,' he said. Critics see irony, but for Trump, it's all part of a grand beautification plan. He's pledged to 're-grass' D.C. parks 'with the best guys in the country.' Love it or hate it, Trump's grass talk reveals a president who often sounds more like a small-town mayor than a world leader—obsessed with the ground beneath his feet.
why_it_matters: Trump's micro-focus on grass suggests how a leader's personal obsessions can shape the physical and symbolic landscape of the nation, influencing how the presidency is perceived and how public spaces are maintained.

background_read: Donald Trump, before entering politics, spent decades as a real estate developer and golf course owner, giving him unusual hands-on experience with landscaping. His attention to the White House grounds echoes a long tradition: presidents often leave their mark on the 18-acre estate. For example, John F. Kennedy hired a designer to reshape the Rose Garden, and Michelle Obama planted a vegetable garden. The helicopter Trump references is Marine One, the official aircraft for the president, typically a large Sikorsky helicopter that can blast turf during landings. Scotts Miracle-Gro, the company whose lawn expert met with Trump, is a major American brand known for its grass seed and fertilizers. While heads of state usually focus on diplomacy or legislation, Trump's grass fixation shows how a leader's private passions can become a surprising part of the public record.

perspectives.description: Trump's attention to lawn care could lead to improved public spaces in Washington, D.C., and his business experience might bring efficient management to grounds maintenance. Supporters see a leader who cares about aesthetics and details.

Critics argue that a president obsessing over grass while major national and international issues loom is a sign of misplaced priorities. The destruction of historic lawns like the Rose Garden damages cultural heritage and disregards tradition.

Presidential preoccupations often reflect their pre-political lives; Trump's grass fixation highlights the ways personal background shapes executive focus. This tendency is not unique—many presidents have had pet projects that seemed trivial but symbolized broader values or personal identity.

The planned re-grassing of D.C. parks could become a legacy project, but future administrations might reverse the changes. The episode may prompt lasting debate over how the White House grounds are managed and preserved as a public trust for all Americans.
